    The annotation model

    Source: vignettes/annotation-model.Rmd
    annotation-model.Rmd

    hyperannotatR represents an annotation as a small hierarchy of plain R objects, each a validated layer built on the one below. This vignette describes that model: the pixel coordinate system every object shares, the four nested classes, how geometric validity is checked and repaired, and how coordinates move between pyramid levels. These few conventions are enough to use the rest of the package with confidence.

    The coordinate system

    Every coordinate in hyperannotatR is an image pixel coordinate. The origin sits at the top-left corner of the image, x increases to the right, and y increases downward – the raster convention used by cameras, microscopes, and most image libraries. This is the mirror image of the GIS convention, in which y increases upward. When exchanging geometry with GIS-oriented tooling, flip at the boundary with at_flip_y().

    A pixel is a unit cell, not a point. Pixel (i, j) – row i, column j, both one-based – covers the half-open square [j-1, j) x [i-1, i), so its centre lies at (j - 0.5, i - 0.5). Membership follows that centre: a pixel belongs to a region when its centre falls inside the polygon. Boundary ties are evaluated symbolically at (x + epsilon, y + epsilon^2) as epsilon tends to zero from above. For axis-aligned rectangles this is the half-open [lower, upper) rule; it also defines sloping edges deterministically. Holes use ring parity and MultiPolygon components combine by union. Points instead select their half-open containing cells, so point (5,5) belongs to matrix row 6, column 6. Masks and extraction share these rules.

            x increases  --->
      0     1     2     3
    0 +-----+-----+-----+
      |     |     |     |     pixel (row 2, col 2)
    1 +-----+-----+-----+     covers [1, 2) x [1, 2)
 y  |     |  o  |     |       centre = (1.5, 1.5)   <- "o"
 |  |     | 1.5 |     |
 v  2 +-----+-----+-----+
      |     |     |     |
    3 +-----+-----+-----+

    A rectangle spanning columns and rows 2–3 makes the rule concrete. Testing the centres of the four pixels along the diagonal, only those whose centre falls inside are matched:

    sq <- at_roi_rect(1, 1, 3, 3, label = "cell")
at_roi_contains(sq, x = c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5), y = c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5))
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

    The object hierarchy

    Annotations are built from four nested classes: annot_roi -> annot_layer -> annot_project -> annot_session.

    An annot_roi is a single region of interest: an sf geometry (a point, polygon, ellipse, and so on) stored in pixel coordinates at a declared pyramid level, together with a label, a unique identifier, and provenance.

    rect <- at_roi_rect(120, 150, 260, 290, label = "tumour")
rect
#> <annot_roi> tumour (POLYGON)
#> id: "roi_000000002"  |  level: 0  |  source: manual
#> bbox: [120, 150] - [260, 290]
at_roi_area(rect)
#> [1] 19600

    An annot_layer groups ROIs that share a controlled label vocabulary and a drawing style. Layers are the unit of visibility, locking, and z-order. Adding an ROI never mutates the input; it returns an extended copy.

    regions <- at_layer("regions", labels = c("tumour", "stroma"))
regions <- at_layer_add(regions, rect)
regions <- at_layer_add(regions, at_roi_circle(400, 120, r = 40, label = "stroma"))
regions
#> <annot_layer> regions
#> ROIs: 2  |  labels: "tumour" and "stroma"
#> visible: TRUE  |  locked: FALSE  |  z: 1

    An annot_project binds one image to a named set of layers and records provenance. It is the object you query, validate, rasterise, and export. at_rois() returns a tidy table in which coordinates, areas, and centroids are expressed at level 0. The level column is therefore always 0; source_level records where each ROI was originally defined. Older query tables used level for that provenance: consumers must switch to source_level when they need the stored level. Empty tables have the same schema. Querying never changes the stored ROI.

    img  <- at_example_image("tissue")
proj <- at_project(img, regions, name = "demo")
at_layers(proj)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   name    n_rois labels    visible locked     z
#>   <chr>    <int> <list>    <lgl>   <lgl>  <int>
#> 1 regions      2 <chr [2]> TRUE    FALSE      1
at_rois(proj)[, c("roi_id", "layer", "label", "geom_type", "level", "source_level", "area_px")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   roi_id        layer   label  geom_type level source_level area_px
#>   <chr>         <chr>   <chr>  <chr>     <int>        <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 roi_000000002 regions tumour POLYGON       0            0  19600 
#> 2 roi_000000003 regions stroma POLYGON       0            0   5018.

    Finally, an annot_session wraps a queue of images with a manifest, a cursor, and shared label and layer templates, so a project can be materialised, annotated, and saved for each image in turn.

    sess <- at_example_session(3)
at_session_status(sess)[, c("idx", "name", "status")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>     idx name     status 
#>   <int> <chr>    <chr>  
#> 1     1 image_01 pending
#> 2     2 image_02 pending
#> 3     3 image_03 pending

    Geometry validity and repair

    Every constructor finalises its geometry: the CRS is cleared and, if the result is topologically invalid, sf::st_make_valid() is applied with a warning. ROIs you build in R are therefore valid by construction. Geometry that arrives from elsewhere – imported GeoJSON, a QuPath project, a hand-edited file – carries no such guarantee, so hyperannotatR offers an explicit audit.

    at_check_geometry() reports one row per problem across the whole project: self-intersections, zero-area or degenerate rings, duplicate vertices, reversed hole winding, NA coordinates, and vertices outside the image bounds, each tagged by severity and by whether it can be repaired automatically. Here we add one ROI that spills past the image edge and one with a duplicated vertex:

    proj <- at_add_roi(proj, "regions", at_roi_rect(430, 430, 620, 620, label = "tumour"))
dup  <- at_roi_polygon(
  matrix(c(0, 0, 0, 0, 40, 0, 40, 40, 0, 40), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE),
  label = "stroma"
)
proj <- at_add_roi(proj, "regions", dup)
at_check_geometry(proj)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   roi_id        issue              severity fixable
#>   <chr>         <chr>              <chr>    <lgl>  
#> 1 roi_000000004 out_of_bounds      warning  TRUE   
#> 2 roi_000000005 duplicate_vertices warning  TRUE

    at_fix_geometry() repairs what it can: here it drops the duplicated vertex and pulls the rectangle that spills past the edge back inside the image bounds. Issues it cannot repair, such as zero-area rings or NA coordinates, are left in place and reported. To confine a single ROI to the image without the other repairs, use at_clamp().

    proj <- at_fix_geometry(proj)
#> ✔ Repaired 2 ROIs.
at_check_geometry(proj)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 4
#> # ℹ 4 variables: roi_id <chr>, issue <chr>, severity <chr>, fixable <lgl>

    Pyramid levels and coordinate transforms

    Whole-slide and multiplex images are pyramids: the same scene stored at several resolutions. An ROI records the level at which its coordinates were digitised in its level field, so a region drawn on a low-resolution overview is never silently misread as full-resolution pixels. Keeping the declared level makes every coordinate unambiguous and every transform reversible.

    Two functions move coordinates between levels. at_roi_rescale() assumes an exact power-of-two pyramid and needs no image: going from level 0 to level 2 divides coordinates by four.

    r0 <- at_roi_rect(0, 0, 100, 100, label = "a")
r2 <- at_roi_rescale(r0, from_level = 0, to_level = 2)
at_roi_bbox(r2)
#> [1]  0  0 25 25

    at_transform() instead uses the real per-level dimensions of an image, so it is exact for pyramids with any downsampling ratio. For the bundled multiplex example, whose levels measure 512, 256, and 128 pixels, the two approaches agree:

    mimg <- at_example_image("multiplex")
at_dims(mimg, level = 0)
#> [1] 512 512
at_dims(mimg, level = 2)
#> [1] 128 128
at_roi_bbox(at_transform(r0, from_level = 0, to_level = 2, img = mimg))
#> [1]  0  0 25 25

    Coordinates can round-trip through pyramid levels within floating-point precision (relative tolerance 1e-12).

    Computations that change levels require the actual image dimensions. Pass image = img to standalone masks, pixel-area measurements, set operations, and distance/overlap measurements, or use a project that carries its image. A bare ROI’s dimensions do not establish a pyramid scale. Set operations and intersection predicates can operate on standalone ROIs at the same stored level; mixed levels require image metadata. With image metadata, set-operation results use level 0. Distance and pairwise overlap areas always use level 0.

    The companion Masks vignette shows how these annotations are rasterised – applying the pixel-centre rule above – into binary, labelled, and multi-class integer masks.
